div.div:
Precomputed, once.
A query never re-reads the PDF — the expensive work (loading, splitting, embedding) already happened at upload time.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 332px; height: 1px; padding-top: 751px; margin-left: 388px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Why the SAME model?
Two different embedding models produce vectors in two different spaces. Distances between them would be meaningless, so retrieval would return nonsense.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 282px; height: 1px; padding-top: 751px; margin-left: 818px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Only top-k reaches the LLM.
5 pages, not 1000. That is what keeps the call affordable and the answer focused on the right context.

div.div: In LangChain terms: Document Loader → Text Splitter → Vector Store → Retriever are the four pieces of the Indexes component; the embedding model and the Brain are both the Models component; wiring the whole path together is a Chain.
